Seamus Heaney's Beowulf is an English verse translation of the Old English epic that combines literal fidelity with poetic vivacity, rendering the Anglo-Saxon alliterative tradition into modern English verse. Published in nineteen ninety-nine when Heaney was already Ireland's most celebrated poet, his translation won the Whitbread Book of the Year and became the contemporary standard, bringing the ancient poem alive for readers while preserving its archaic resonance and violent intensity.

Heaney based his translation on the Old English alliterative tradition rather than end rhyme. He uses half-alliteration, sprung rhythm, and contemporary diction to approximate the feel of the original meter without reproducing it exactly. His edition presents Old English on the left page and English on the right, a bilingual format that allows readers to check the original against Heaney's version and appreciate his choices. His language is muscular, concrete, and sometimes violent, deploying Irish-English dialect words and archaic terms that give the poem an ancient-yet-living feel.

Heaney's introduction connects the epic to Irish nationalist and literary politics, reading Beowulf as a poem about cultural survival and the power of language to preserve the dead. His version eclipsed earlier twentieth-century translations and established itself as the Beowulf for contemporary non-specialist readers. It won the nineteen ninety-nine Whitbread Book of the Year award and remains the most widely assigned Beowulf translation in universities, shaping how tens of thousands of students experience the poem.
